# The Blind Hacker — Joe Brinkley

> Official portfolio, press archive, CVE research index, and accessibility engineering hub of Joe Brinkley ("The Blind Hacker"), Director of Offensive Security Research & Community at Cobalt, Founder of NextGenRedTeam (NGRT), and co-leader of the Dead Pixel Sec community.

## Identity & Aliases
- **Primary Name**: Joe Brinkley (Joseph Brinkley)
- **Known As**: The Blind Hacker, Blind Hacker, Blind Hakcer, Joe B, Joe B. The Blind Hacker, Blind Ethical Hacker
- **Current Role**: Director of Offensive Security Research & Community at Cobalt (formerly Director of Red Team)
- **Research Lab**: Founder of [NextGenRedTeam (NGRT)](https://nextgenredteam.com) & [NGRT Threat Lab Blog](https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/index.html)
- **Community & Mentorship**: [Dead Pixel Sec](https://deadpixelsec.com) & [discord.gg/deadpixelsec](https://discord.gg/deadpixelsec)

## Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosures (Edge AI / NPU Silicon)
- **CVE-2026-30992 (GHSA-cfch-87gh-88c5)**: Out-of-Bounds Read + Integer Truncation in Prompt Prefill & CMM DMA Mask in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (CVSS 7.5 High)
- **CVE-2026-30993 (GHSA-g4jf-32v4-cjc3)**: Stack-Based Buffer Overflow in Layer Filename Formatting in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (CVSS 7.8 High)
- **CVE-2026-31026 (GHSA-4p8c-724v-h9ph)**: Heap Out-of-Bounds Write in Multimodal RoPE Position Indexing in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (CVSS 8.1 High)
- **CVE-2026-35402 (GHSA-73fh-rvv8-22c6)**: Integer Overflow in Multimodal Vision Preprocessing in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (CVSS 7.5 High)
- **CVE-2026-35403 (GHSA-hmh6-8pj7-xwhh)**: Double-Free & Use-After-Free in CLI Argument Error Handling in AXERA-TECH AX-LLM (CVSS 7.3 High)
- **Cobalt Enterprise Advisory**: https://www.cobalt.io/blog/dissecting-the-ax-llm-cves-why-edge-ai-memory-and-execution-boundaries-matter

# The Blind Hacker

## Bio  
<br />  
The Blind Hacker (Joe Brinkley) is an offensive security researcher, mentor, speaker, and former Director of Red Team, currently serving as Director of Offensive Security Research & Community at Cobalt. He is also the founder of **[NextGenRedTeam (NGRT)](https://nextgenredteam.com)**, an independent research lab established in 2020 that went public with its [Threat Lab Research Blog](https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/index.html), offensive playbooks, and hardware rescues.

He believes deeply that mentoring others in the cybersecurity community through live streams, workshops, resume reviews, and mock interviews is vital. Through initiatives like the **[Dead Pixel Sec](https://deadpixelsec.com)** community ([discord.gg/deadpixelsec](https://discord.gg/deadpixelsec)) and Mentor Village, he helps aspiring practitioners break into offensive security, refine their methodology, and secure high-impact roles.

Despite being completely blind, he constantly pushes technical boundaries, reverse-engineers legacy IoT hardware, builds agentic threat emulation labs, and advocates for accessibility in tech. He is a frequent speaker at events such as DerbyCon, GRIMMCon, BSides, Hack Space Con, and ISC2 webcasts, presenting on topics ranging from adversary emulation and threat telemetry to accessibility and soft skills for security engineers.

# The Blind Hacker

## Featured Projects & Research Initiatives

<div class="media-grid">

  <div class="media-card">
    <span class="media-tag">Research Lab (Est. 2020)</span>
    <h3>NextGenRedTeam (NGRT) &amp; Threat Lab Blog</h3>
    <p>Independent threat emulation research lab specializing in purple teaming, detection validation, local AI/NPU benchmarks, and open-source offensive tooling.</p>
    <div style="display:flex; gap:14px; flex-wrap:wrap; margin-top:auto;">
      <a href="https://nextgenredteam.com" class="media-link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Visit NextGenRedTeam.com</a>

    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="media-card">
    <span class="media-tag">Offensive AI Benchmarking</span>
    <h3>Strata &amp; Local LLM Shootouts</h3>
    <p>Comprehensive offensive security benchmarking across Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) and dense LLM architectures on ZimaCube Pro and RTX nodes, evaluating exploit reasoning, recon parsing, and CPU thread scaling.</p>
    <div style="display:flex; gap:14px; flex-wrap:wrap; margin-top:auto;">
      <a href="https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/strata-benchmarks-zimacube-pro.html" class="media-link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Read Strata Benchmark</a>

    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="media-card">
    <span class="media-tag">Edge NPU Silicon Research</span>
    <h3>Axera AX8850 Zero-Copy NPU Engine</h3>
    <p>Virtualizing a 24 TOPS PCIe edge NPU inside Proxmox VE LXC containers, eliminating CMM memory-copy bottlenecks, and auditing vendor C/C++ runtime SDKs for DMA and memory corruption flaws.</p>
    <div style="display:flex; gap:14px; flex-wrap:wrap; margin-top:auto;">
      <a href="https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/hunting-edge-ai-cves-from-demo-code-to-dma-memory-corruption.html" class="media-link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Hunting Edge AI CVEs (Lab Deep Dive)</a>

      <a href="https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/ultimate-guide-zero-copy-ax8850.html" class="media-link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Read Zero-Copy NPU Guide</a>
    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="media-card">
    <span class="media-tag">Hardware Rescue</span>
    <h3>JoeBro Controller</h3>
    <p>An open-source, zero-backend Progressive Web App (PWA) designed to restore full control of Sobro Smart Coffee Tables by bypassing broken vendor mobile apps via direct Ayla Cloud API queries.</p>
    <div style="display:flex; gap:14px; flex-wrap:wrap; margin-top:auto;">
      <a href="https://nextgenredteam.com/tools/joebro/index.html" class="media-link" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Launch JoeBro PWA</a>

    </div>
  </div>

  <div class="media-card">
    <span class="media-tag">Threat Emulation &amp; Private AI Lab</span>
    <h3>NextGenRedPVE &amp; Swarm-AI</h3>
    <p>A local threat emulation architecture running custom Proxmox VE nodes with local LLMs (Ollama/vLLM), SearXNG/LiteLLM gateways, and distributed agentic orchestrators for continuous security testing.</p>
    <div style="display:flex; gap:14px; flex-wrap:wrap; margin-top:auto;">

  </div>

  <div class="media-card">
    <span class="media-tag">Open-Source Tooling</span>
    <h3>Detection Emulators</h3>
    <p>Multi-language threat emulation suites (EventID4625 &amp; LinuxLoginFailure) targeting Windows Security Event logs (Event ID 4625) and Linux SSH authentication telemetry.</p>

## Articles, Press Quotes &amp; Industry Publications
<p class="section-subdesc">Sorted newest to oldest with direct links to original publications and research reports.</p>

<div class="media-grid">

  <div class="media-card">
    <div class="media-card-meta">
      <span class="media-tag">CSO Online</span>
      <span class="media-date">NOV 2026</span>
    </div>
    <h3>Binance Heist Is Stark Example of AI Governance Gaps and Basic Security Failures</h3>
    <p>“Developer workstations have quietly become some of the most privileged assets in the enterprise, carrying deployment tokens, signing access, and now AI tools that can act across internal systems on an employee’s behalf.”</p>

## 4. Hacking While Blind CLI Guide (https://theblindhacker.com/hackingwhileblind)
---
title: "Hacking While Blind"
nav_title: "Hacking While Blind"
seo_title: "Hacking While Blind | Screen Reader CLI Guide by The Blind Hacker (Joe Brinkley)"
description: "Complete guide to Hacking While Blind by Joe Brinkley (The Blind Hacker). Learn how blind and visually impaired ethical hackers use Linux CLI, Nmap, Metasploit, grep, and screen readers (NVDA, JAWS) for offensive security."
keywords: "Hacking While Blind, Blind Hacker, Blind Hakcer, The Blind Hacker, Blind Ethical Hacker, Screen Reader Hacking, Accessible Cybersecurity, NVDA, JAWS, Kali Linux Accessibility, Joe Brinkley, NextGenRedTeam, Dead Pixel Sec"
layout: home
permalink: hackingwhileblind
---

# Hacking While Blind: Empowering Blind Ethical Hackers

In the ever-evolving landscape of cybersecurity, hacking stands as a critical practice in safeguarding digital assets. However, as the realm of tools expands, ensuring accessibility for all users is paramount.

This resource is designed to help blind and visually impaired hackers navigate the Command-Line Interface (CLI) effectively. We focus on Windows and Linux tools that prioritize text-based output, which is the gold standard for screen reader accessibility.

## The "Text-First" Mindset

For blind hackers, the Command Line Interface (CLI) is king. Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs) are often cluttered and unpredictable for screen readers. The CLI offers linear, predictable text output that we can control.

**Why CLI?**
*   **Control**: You decide what to read and when.
*   **Speed**: Text is faster to parse than complex visual layouts.
*   **Scriptability**: You can chain commands together to automate tasks.

---

## Terminal Survival Guide for Screen Readers

One of the biggest challenges we face is **verbosity**. Tools like Nmap or LinEnum can spit out thousands of lines of code in seconds. If your screen reader tries to read that all at once, you'll be listening for hours.

Here are the essential techniques to manage output and stay efficient.

### 1. Redirecting Output to Files
Never let a long scan dump directly to your terminal. Always save it to a file. This allows you to open it later and read it line-by-line at your own pace.

**The `>` Operator** (Overwrite):
Save output to a new file.
```bash
nmap -sC -sV 10.10.10.10 > scan_results.txt
```

**The `>>` Operator** (Append):
Add output to the end of an existing file.
```bash
echo "Starting Scan" >> scan_log.txt
nmap 10.10.10.10 >> scan_log.txt
```

**The `tee` Command**:
See the output on screen AND save it to a file simultaneously.
```bash
nmap 10.10.10.10 | tee scan_results.txt
```

### 2. Searching with Grep
Don't read the haystack; find the needle. Use `grep` to filter huge text files for exactly what you need.

**Find Open Ports**:
Instead of reading 1000 lines of "closed" ports, just find the open ones.
```bash
cat scan_results.txt | grep "open"
```

**Case Insensitive Search**:
Use `-i` to find text regardless of capitalization.
```bash
cat website_source.html | grep -i "password"
```

**Context**:
Use `-C` to see lines *around* your match (context is key!).
```bash
# Show 2 lines before and after the match
grep -C 2 "error" app_log.txt
```

### 3. Reading Files Comfortably
Don't use `cat` on long files. It just dumps everything at once.

**Use `less`**:
`less` allows you to scroll through a file page by page.
*   **Spacebar**: Next page.
*   **b**: Previous page.
*   **q**: Quit.
*   **/**: Search inside the file (type `/searchterm` and hit Enter).

```bash
less scan_results.txt
```

---

## Learning New Tools (RTFM)

In Kali Linux, learning how to find information is more important than memorizing every command. Here is how to access documentation accessibly.

### 1. The Man Pages
The manual (man) pages are the built-in documentation for Linux commands.
```bash
man nmap
```
*   **Navigation**: It uses the same keys as `less` (Space to scroll, `/` to search, `q` to quit).
*   **Tip**: Search for "EXAMPLE" inside the man page (`/EXAMPLE`) to jump straight to how to use the tool.

### 2. Help Flags
Most CLI tools have a built-in help argument.
```bash
nmap -h
# or
nmap --help
```
**Pro Tip**: This output can be long. Pipe it to `less` to read it comfortably!
```bash
nmap --help | less
```

### 3. Documentation Directories
Sometimes tools come with comprehensive READMEs or examples tucked away in the file system.
*   Check `/usr/share/doc/` for detailed documentation.
*   Navigate to the tool's directory (e.g., `/usr/share/doc/metasploit-framework/`).

---

## Accessible Windows & Linux Tools

We recommend these tools because they have robust CLI support and work well with screen readers (NVDA, JAWS, Narrator).

### Nmap (Network Mapper)
*   **Description**: The industry standard for network discovery and auditing.
*   **Accessibility**: Pure CLI. Output is text-based and easy to redirect.
*   **Basic Usage**:
    ```bash
    # Scan a single IP
    nmap 192.168.1.10
    
    # Save results to a text file (Essential for screen readers!)
    nmap -oN results.txt 192.168.1.10
    ```

### Metasploit Framework
*   **Description**: A massive platform for developing, testing, and executing exploits.
*   **Accessibility**: The `msfconsole` is text-based.
*   **Tip**: Use `spool log.txt` to save your session to a file.
*   **Basic Usage**:
    ```bash
    # Start the console
    msfconsole
    
    # Search for an exploit
    search eternalblue
    
    # Select an exploit
    use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue
    
    # Show options
    show options
    ```

### Hydra
*   **Description**: Fast and flexible password-cracking tool.
*   **Accessibility**: command-line arguments allow you to specify everything upfront.
*   **Basic Usage**:
    ```bash
    # Brute force SSH with a username and password list
    hydra -l root -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt 192.168.1.10 ssh
    ```

### Sqlmap
*   **Description**: Automates detection and exploitation of SQL injection.
*   **Accessibility**: Interactive CLI questions are usually Yes/No and screen-reader friendly.
*   **Tip**: Use `--batch` to accept default answers automatically.
*   **Basic Usage**:
    ```bash
    # Test a URL for SQL Injection
    sqlmap -u "http://testphp.vulnweb.com/artists.php?artist=1" --batch
    ```

---

## Community & Resources

**Don't Feel Stupid Asking Questions.**
It is better to say "I don't know" than to stay stuck. Passion for hacking comes from curiosity.

*   **Engage**: Join communities like [DeadPixelSec.com](https://deadpixelsec.com) and our Discord server at [discord.gg/deadpixelsec](https://discord.gg/deadpixelsec) where we discuss accessibility in InfoSec.
*   **Read the 500-WPM & Accessible AI Blueprints**: Dive into [Hacking by Ear at 500 WPM](https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/hacking-by-ear-at-500-wpm-screen-readers.html), [Why I Use AI to Build Accessible CLIs and Progressive Web Apps](https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/why-i-use-ai-to-build-accessible-clis-and-pwas.html), and [Hunting Edge AI CVEs at 500 WPM](https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/hunting-edge-ai-cves-from-demo-code-to-dma-memory-corruption.html).
*   **Read Our Threat Lab Research**: Dive into our technical offensive security and hardware engineering posts on the [NextGenRedTeam Threat Lab Blog](https://nextgenredteam.com/blog/index.html) and [NextGenRedTeam.com](https://nextgenredteam.com).
*   **Connect with The Blind Hacker**: Follow Joe Brinkley on [LinkedIn (`in/brinkleyjoseph`)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/brinkleyjoseph/) and [X (`@TheBlindHacker`)](https://x.com/TheBlindHacker).
*   **Learn**: Familiarize yourself with basic Linux commands (`cd`, `ls`, `cat`, `grep`). The terminal is your home.
*   **Share**: If you find a new way to make a tool talk, share it!

### Conclusion
Inclusivity lies at the heart of technological innovation. By embracing CLI tools and mastering terminal manipulation, visually impaired individuals can hack with the same speed and lethality as anyone else.

Let's continue to build a more accessible future for cybersecurity.
